introduction.text: The Basilica Hilariana is a small, partially underground basilica on Rome’s Caelian Hill, built in the mid‑2nd century by pearl merchant Manius Publicius Ilarius for the dendrophores, a cult linked to Magna Mater and Attis. Its modest size and distinctive mosaic decoration illustrate the adaptation of civic basilica architecture for religious use in late antiquity.

history.description: Construction of the basilica in the mid‑2nd century for the dendrophores cult.
Modification of the complex in the 3rd century.
Abandonment of the basilica in the 7th century, possibly after an earthquake.
An earthquake in 618 AD may have contributed to the basilica’s abandonment.

design.description: The basilica was partially underground, accessed by twelve marble steps leading to a vestibule.
The vestibule featured black and white mosaics depicting an eye struck by a spear surrounded by birds and animals.
A threshold with a footprint motif led to a room containing a basin and the base of a statue dedicated to Ilarius.

art.description: Mosaic iconography of an eye struck by a spear, a motif associated with the cult of Magna Mater.
Mosaic depiction of birds and animals surrounding the spear, reflecting the dendrophores’ symbolic imagery.
Footprint motif in the threshold mosaic, indicating a symbolic passage or rite.
